subtype: Parents × Divorce or conflict at home [Receiver]
passage:
A kettle screaming at midnight while Ammi and Abbu shouted in the next room: that's the sound I still hear. I'm Nazia, and I'm telling you this, Bidisha, because you asked why I go quiet when couples argue in the canteen.

They separated last year. At first I tried to fix it. I carried messages. Abbu said, "Tell your mother," and Ammi said, "Tell your father," and I felt like a bridge with both ends on fire. I even wrote each of them a long letter about being kinder.

Then my aunt said, "You're their daughter, not their referee." It was the first time I could breathe.

I stopped carrying messages. I call both of them every Sunday and tell each I love them and won't discuss the other. It still hurts. But I sleep now.

qa.q: When did Nazia's parents separate?
qa.a: Last year.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel while carrying messages between her parents?
qa.a: Like a bridge with both ends on fire, pulled and burned from both sides.

qa.q: What boundary did Nazia set with her parents?
qa.a: She stopped carrying messages, kept calling both every Sunday, and told each of them she loves them but will not discuss the other.

qa.q: What did Nazia's aunt see that Nazia hadn't?
qa.a: That Nazia was taking on a job that belonged to the parents, being their referee instead of their daughter.

grounding: Nazia's parents' fights and separation land on her; she stops trying to fix them and loves both while keeping healthy distance.

"Amma, can I chop the onions?"

"You? You'll cry." Rukmini pushed the board over anyway.

"Show me how you make the sambar, the way Paati did."

"Tamarind first. Not too much." A pause. "Why are you asking?"

"Because we usually eat and go to our rooms. I'd like to know how you do things."

Rukmini stirred for a while. "Your father and I never learned to talk. In our house you just ate and worked."

"I know you pay for everything, Amma. I'm not complaining. I just miss you."

"...Hand me the curry leaves." She smiled without looking up.

That week Kamal also asked his lab professor if they could meet once a month, so there would be another person to talk things over with.

qa.q: What does Rukmini say to add first when making the sambar?
qa.a: The tamarind, and not too much.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling and wanting when asking to chop the onions?
qa.a: Kamal misses Amma and feels lonely for closeness, since they usually eat and go to their rooms, and wants to learn how she does things.

qa.q: What other step does Kamal take besides cooking with Amma?
qa.a: Kamal asks the lab professor to meet once a month, so there is another mentor to talk things over with.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt during this conversation?
qa.a: Perhaps awkward but moved. She admits that she and her husband never learned to talk, and she smiles without looking up.

grounding: Kamal's parents provide but rarely talk; Kamal reaches out through cooking and asks for another mentor.

passage:
I'm Neel, their cousin, and I was staying at Kiran and Salma's flat over Diwali. Salma had just cleared the civil services prelims, and the whole family kept saying "Our Salma" every few minutes.

Kiran laughed and passed the sweets round, but I saw Kiran leave the room twice and stand on the balcony. Later, in the kitchen, Kiran said something short to Salma: "Everything is about you this week." Salma looked shocked. "I didn't ask for it. It's hard for me too." Kiran didn't apologise, but sat down.

The next day I heard Kiran tell their mother, "It stings when you introduce Salma first." Their mother went quiet, then said she hadn't realised.

I can't say what Kiran feels inside, but the trips to the balcony stopped.

qa.q: What had Salma just cleared?
qa.a: The civil services prelims.

qa.q: What might Kiran's trips to the balcony suggest, and how sure can Neel be?
qa.a: They may suggest a stinging sense of being overlooked, but Neel only saw behaviour and cannot be sure of Kiran's inner state.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that helped with the envy?
qa.a: Kiran said how it felt, first to Salma and then to their mother, instead of competing for approval.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt about the attention that week?
qa.a: Uncomfortable or pressured. Salma says "I didn't ask for it. It's hard for me too."

grounding: Kiran envies a sibling who seems the family's favourite and, instead of sabotage, talks to sibling and mother about how it stings, seen by a cousin.

passage:
Come here, child. You look like someone whose sister has gone quiet. I'm Pooja, and mine did too, years ago.

When I won the government scholarship, my sister Vasudha stopped sitting with me at dinner. "Now you'll be the pride of the house," she said, "and I'm just the one who stays."

My first thought was to hide the letter and stop talking about college. I didn't. I told her, "I won't pretend I'm not happy. But I want to hear how this feels for you." She cried a little. She said she'd been told to marry at twenty while I got to study.

I didn't boast and I didn't lecture. I listened. When I got my first pay I paid for her sewing course. It took years before we laughed together again, but we did.

qa.q: What did Pooja pay for with her first pay?
qa.a: Vasudha's sewing course.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she stopped sitting with Pooja at dinner?
qa.a: Left behind and resentful. She said, "I'm just the one who stays," and told Pooja she'd been told to marry at twenty.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't hide her scholarship or boast. She said she was happy, asked how it felt for Vasudha, and listened without lecturing.

qa.q: How might Pooja have seen her scholarship after hearing Vasudha's side?
qa.a: Pooja probably saw that her chance to study came with a cost her sister felt, which is why she listened and later paid for Vasudha's sewing course.

grounding: Pooja's sister resents her success; Pooja does not shrink, stays generous and listens to her sister's feelings, told by an elder.

passage:
Rain hammered the auto's canopy, and Parveen's train to Nagpur left in forty minutes. Imran gripped the seat in front. "Let me come with you. I'll sit in another compartment."

"Bhaiya, it's a two-hour interview. Alone."

He listed the problems: the crowded station, the ticket checker, her phone battery. She laughed a little, then didn't. "You said the same before I went to hostel. I lived."

Imran wanted to shout, "Because I called you every night." He swallowed it. "Take my power bank. Message me when you board and when you arrive. Take the ladies' coach if it feels better. But you decide."

"That I can do," Parveen said.

At the platform he handed her a packet of biscuits, not another warning. When the train pulled out, his hands were shaking, and he let them.

qa.q: How long until Parveen's train left?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling in the auto, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Anxious. He gripped the seat, listed one problem after another and wanted to shout.

qa.q: Which choice helped, and why?
qa.a: Offering the power bank and messages while leaving the decisions to Parveen. It gave guidance without taking over.

qa.q: How might Parveen see Imran's worry?
qa.a: As too much at first, since she has managed before. But she accepts his help once it stops being control and lets her decide.

grounding: Imran wants to shield his younger sister from mistakes and, under time pressure, gives guidance while letting her decide.

Monday. Lalit's message came at eleven at night: "Bhai, can you send some for the trip? Also, science elective or commerce?" It was the third money request that month. Chaitanya sent it, then lay awake, feeling used, and guilty for feeling it.

Saturday, two weeks later. When Lalit asked again, Chaitanya called instead of transferring. "I'll help with the trip once. But you choose the elective. What did you enjoy in class?" Lalit stammered, then talked for ten minutes about his physics teacher. "Sounds like you already know," Chaitanya said.

Sunday, a month after that. Lalit sent a photo of his first earnings from the bookshop. "Bought my own textbooks. Still want advice on one thing 🙂" Chaitanya smiled and typed, "Ask."

qa.q: What did Lalit buy with his own earnings?
qa.a: His own textbooks.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel after sending the money on Monday?
qa.a: Used, and also guilty for feeling used.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya change on Saturday, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Chaitanya called instead of transferring, helped once, and asked Lalit to make the elective choice. A month later Lalit was earning and buying his own textbooks.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when asked to choose the elective himself?
qa.a: Nervous, since he stammered at first. But talking about his physics teacher shows that being trusted helped him find his own answer.

grounding: A younger sibling leans on Chaitanya for money and decisions; Chaitanya supports kindly while encouraging his independence, across three days.

passage:
Dear Bhavna,

Mummy asked me last night where you were on Saturday. I said you were out with friends, which is true, and I said nothing about Ronit. That is yours to tell, and I'll keep it.

But I need to be honest with you, so you don't hear it as a betrayal later. Last month I told her you were "at the library" when you were riding on the back of his bike at night without a helmet. I felt sick afterwards. I won't lie about that again. If she asks, I'll tell her to ask you.

Please wear a helmet, or don't go, and please tell Mummy the rest when you're ready. I'm on your side, even when I sound like your worst enemy.

Minakshi

qa.q: What did Minakshi tell Mummy about Saturday?
qa.a: That Bhavna was out with friends.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel after saying Bhavna was "at the library", and why?
qa.a: Minakshi felt guilty and sick, because it was a lie that covered for risky night rides, and it went against Minakshi's own honesty.

qa.q: What line does Minakshi draw?
qa.a: Minakshi keeps Bhavna's private matters private, such as Ronit, but will not lie to cover the risky night rides.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Perhaps exposed or annoyed, but also relieved that private things stay hers. "I'm on your side" may soften it.

grounding: Minakshi covers for her sibling with their parents but protects only privacy, not harmful behaviour.

passage:
On the last Friday of the month, with the electricity bill due by five and Papa's clinic visit the next morning, Gurleen stood in the bank queue doing sums and stewing. For two years she had done the paperwork, the pharmacy runs and the phone calls to relatives. Nilesh sent money and "good luck" messages. She had been keeping score in silence, and today it sat like a lump in her chest.

When the queue cleared she called him instead of texting. "Nilesh, I'm not angry, I'm tired. I do nearly everything for Papa and Mummy. Can we sit down on Sunday and divide it?"

He was silent. "I thought you liked being in charge. I'm sorry. I can take the clinic runs and the bills online."

"I'd like that," Gurleen said. She paid the bill with two minutes to spare.

qa.q: When was the electricity bill due?
qa.a: By five, on the last Friday of the month.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she waited in the bank queue?
qa.a: Tired and resentful. She had been keeping score in silence for two years and it sat like a lump in her chest.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do to avoid an explosion?
qa.a: She called Nilesh, spoke honestly without anger, and proposed sitting down on Sunday to divide the tasks.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have seen the arrangement before the call?
qa.a: He assumed Gurleen liked being in charge. His apology and offer suggest he hadn't realised how much she carried.

grounding: One sibling handles the ageing parents' errands and money more than the other; Gurleen has an honest conversation about fair shares under time pressure.

passage:
"Jomon, are you awake?"

"It's past midnight. What happened?"

"Nothing happened. That's the problem. I made dal today and I didn't know who to send a photo to."

"You could send it to me."

"I'm serious. Since I moved here I keep noticing how often you fixed things: my bike, my laptop, my arguments with Amma."

"You never said thanks."

"I know. I'm saying it now. I miss you being annoying."

"Okay, that's the nicest thing you've ever said. I'm visiting next month with my bad jokes."

"Bring pickle."

"Done."

After the call, Seema sent the photo of the dal anyway.

qa.q: What did Seema cook that day?
qa.a: Dal.

qa.q: What is Seema feeling when calling Jomon, and what shows it?
qa.a: Missing Jomon and realising how much Seema relied on him. Seema calls with "nothing happened" and says "I miss you being annoying".

qa.q: What does Seema do that shows affection openly?
qa.a: Seema says thanks and "I miss you" out loud, and sends the photo of the dal.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel hearing this?
qa.a: Touched, though he teases. He calls it the nicest thing Seema has ever said and plans a visit.

grounding: Distance makes Seema realise how much she relies on her sibling, and she says so out loud and shows up in small ways.

passage:
Maria's draft came back with "Where is your evidence?" circled twice in red. Her face went hot, and there was the old urge to mumble "sorry" and hide.

Professor Simran's office hours were at four. Maria arrived at four sharp with her draft, a page of marked questions and a pen. "You've seen my comments," the professor said.

"I'd like to understand what counts as evidence for this kind of claim," Maria said. "I thought the survey was enough."

"Show me what you'd use instead."

They spent twelve minutes on it. Maria wrote down two sources to read, thanked the professor, and said, "I'll send the revised section by Friday, so you don't have to chase me."

Walking out, her heart was still thumping, but she felt lit up, as if someone had taken her seriously.

qa.q: What time were the professor's office hours?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling on seeing the red comment, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Embarrassed and anxious. Her face went hot and she wanted to mumble "sorry" and hide, though she still went to office hours prepared.

qa.q: How does Maria show she values the professor's time?
qa.a: She arrives at four sharp with questions ready and promises the revised section by Friday so that nobody has to chase her.

qa.q: How might Professor Simran see Maria's visit?
qa.a: As a sign of a serious student who wants to improve. The professor invites Maria to show what she would use instead.

grounding: Maria respects a professor who challenges her, asks questions, accepts correction and treats their time as valuable.
